Author: @jarmokankaanpaa6528
Content: Lutefisk (Norwegian) or lipeäkala (Finnish) is a traditional Scandinavian Christmas dish made from stockfish. The dry stockfish is soaked in a solution of lye and water for several days to soften it, then rinsed in cold water to remove the lye and boiled. It is quite soft and doesn't have much of a taste of its own, so it is served with béchamel sauce and white pepper (and potatoes). Nowadays you can get it ready-to-eat (after boiling), i.e. lye soaked, rinsed and packed (usually in plastic). When I was a kid in Wisconsin, we got it from a Norwegian grocer, though I never actually learned to like it. However, it's originally a Medieval dish and thus something Max might consider trying one day.

Author: @TheResearchMom
Content: Growing up in Romania during communism, we did spend the summer pickling, making preserves and yes, we slaughtered a pig for Christmas. In addition to fresh roasts, we’d send sausages and various cuts to be smoked. Apples were kept in the cellar, same with potatoes and carrots in boxes filled with salt. Onions were similarly cold stored and we’d hang ropes of garlic. My grandma had a freezing cold pantry where we stored lots of jars filled with lovely preserves: berries, rose petals, apricots and peaches and green walnuts. We had huge barrels of pickled cabbage, pickled dill cucumbers, green tomatoes, etc. We kept chickens and turkeys, hence fresh eggs and fresh poultry. Depending where you lived you’d have sheep (they spent summer up in the mountains grazing). And of course, jars of summer honey, pickled mushrooms (they’re delicious). Once we could buy a large freezer we’d freeze lots of veg for stews - no good for salads, unfortunately, but you can’t have everything. Funny enough, we never stuff like frumenty. There was lots of baking and we’d make the traditional mămăligă - a local polenta. And we kept small barrels of feta and wheels of cașcaval (similar to cheddar, I guess). Staying fed in winter involved a lot of work and we didn’t have access to exotic fruits like citrus or pineapple,mangoes, etc. but Danube and Black Sea fish was available, more or less, and everything was pretty much unchanged from medieval times. People outside the cities would hunt - pheasant, rabbits, deer - although it was technically illegal, there were ways around it:-)

Author: @kattkatt744
Content:
14:00 I sort of get the desire to make Stockfish as a food history channel, but it isn't going to happen the right way in a warmer climate like the Californina coast. The Stockfish production process relies up on the freezing winter and spring winds to do the job of the drying. Climate where Stockfish production is done is subarctic or arctic coastal climate, so you will max out at 5C and typicallly for where most of the production is done it will be somewhere at -10C to 5C. Any fermantation that happens isn't done intentionally, it just is whatever the bacteria in the air and general environment does when it lives on a fish left to hang outside in those temperatures. Attemting to make Stockfish outside of this climate you are either going to get fish that is infested with insects for warmer climats or fish that is doesn't dry out the right way in colder climates. And neither is going to have the right bacteria working on them.

If you want to make your own preserved fish in a warmer climate it is better to do the salted and dried version of fish, Saltfish. The two are used for different dishes and can't really be interchanged, but the salted version is at least feasible and meant to be made in the warmer climats, so yo uwill get the right taste.

Edit: By the way if there ever is a Stockfish episode I hope there will be a mention of how every cardinal in 14th and 15th century Roma tried their damndest to be appointed head priest of  the parish of Trondenes in Northern Norway even thoug they would never ever go there because they could collect a ungodly amount of taxes in Stockfish from the fishermen making it belonging to the parish.

Author: @simonmeeds1886
Content: My mother remembered my grandfather (in Lincolnshire, England) keeping pigs and slaughtering one near Christmas. It was butchered and various products would be made: sausages, haslet (pronounced "hayss-lut"), brawn, stuffed chine, etc. Even I remember one of my mother's cousins keeping a pig in a sty on his driveway and having is slaughtered behind the local butcher's shop - that was in the 1970s. (You may have to look up some of the pork dishes I mentioned since they are very local - you can buy something called haslet from UK supermarkets, but it only bears a passing resemblance to the real thing. Real Lincolnshire sausages are very special, and stuffed chine is rare now even in Lincolnshire. When my grandfather had pigs the pork belly seems to have been judged poor meat, and went to his father-in-law. Ironically I now love it, but I'm rarely allowed it for fear of high cholesterol levels. If you want to see an account of the handling of a pig at Christmas you can do worse than one of the chapters in an out-of-print book called "Fungus: the Lincolnshire Cat" by Fred Dobson.

Author: @TheLeonhamm
Content:
Umm? High-fibre wholemeal bread - of rye or wheat or mixed, jam preserves, smoked ham and fish, salted pork, greased goose, small beer, ale, mead - mulled or warmed, distilled alcohol, honey cakes with seeds and nuts, barley gruel and barley water, spelt, wheat, or oat porridge, soups and stews .. with parsnips, beets, turnips, mangels, swedes, some of a neighbour's rabbit for your fowl, stuff sent down as leftovers from the Big House or castle, holy-day boxes donated by the monks or nuns .. and there one has a meagre if largely wholesome mixed ration. Add in the many 'festival' feasts to break up the lonely nights, with dance and tune and merriment - even in the leanest of times, and so the moderately healthy 'peasant' (farm owner or tenant) or farm labourer (shepherd, cow-herder, wall-shorer, and go-for) might get through the fasts (that went with the feasts) and the eking out of the remnants before spring brought the new growth.
All rather precarious of course, and dangerous for the many ill or weak or elderly souls. We are so lucky .. to have Max and the crew to do the experimental tasting of the past for us.
Cheers! ;o)

Author: @Beryllahawk
Content:
Max: I want to try making stockfish.
JOHN TOWNSEND WANTS TO KNOW YOUR LOCATION
(giggling wildly to myself)

Also! This dish is actually in my favorite MMO, too. It's one of the first things you can craft as a Culinarian in Final Fantasy 14, and the recipe made it into their official cookbook. (which is almost as pretty as yours by the way!) Their version is a good bit more fancy though, with cinnamon, nutmeg, and i think dried fruit.
In addition - I was reminded about medlars (which I think had a rather naughty name also but my mind won't recall it, ha!) - but, they were a fruit that would have also been available in late fall or during winter even, and were a kind of food that HAD to remain on the tree in order to actually become edible. I think Sir Jason (of "Modern History TV") mentioned the medlars just wouldn't be any good until they were nearly bad. And I can just imagine late apples, any sort of root vegetable that could be kept cool and dry (another great use for the rafters, smoke won't hurt a carrot one little bit), even dried mushrooms would have been quite a blessing. And with all that egg in there you're getting a lot of protein, and some fat, both of which would most certainly "stick to your ribs" calorically speaking. And even in winter there's so much work to be done, you'd NEED a lot of energy. I'm betting this was a meal eaten more than once a day in the coldest weeks of the year, as folk went out, dealt with livestock, came back in and ate a bowl, then went back out, warmed up, to continue their work.

Author: @pdruiz2005
Content: This seasonality in food also happens in poor nations. My parents grew up in rural Central America and, let me tell you, it was not a fun time with food out in the Central American boonies during the 1960s and 1970s. They only had an abundance of food once they moved to the big city. All this seasonality common to medieval European peasants happened with their food too. But the big difference was that this happened in a tropical climate. So the seasonality was dry-season food and wet-season food. Mangoes, for one, grew in abundance during the wet season. But they were hard to come by during the dry season. Oddly enough pickling is never something that happens in tropical regions and with cuisines that evolved in tropical climes. I, for one, never saw anything pickled until I came to North America. But pickling is quite common in parts of the world with long winters.

Content:
It's funny:  this dish (more-or-less) is a staple of my modern day diet!
I love making pottage with eggs and Cream of Wheat cereal.  I picked up the habit in my twenties, when money was tight (a couple eggs and a serving of Cream of Wheat is very affordable), but it's still an amazingly satisfying comfort food.  It can be given infinite variety by changing up the spices - chilli powder, black powder and onion one day; Italian seasonings another; honey, cinnamon and butter another.
In ye olde days, the on-hand ingredients for pottage would vary every couple of weeks - depending on what herbs were in season and so forth.  I'm not at all surprised that many peasants lived quite happily on this basic - but extremely variable - dish.

Content:
This video really makes me think of Farthest Frontier, settlement survival game from the creators of Grim Dawn.

You lead a group of settlers to build a, well, settlement. You start with simple shelters and upgrade in a fashion similar to Age of Empires games. The part that connects is food production: in the game you have hunters, fishermen and foragers, and what they bring can be preserved: fish and meat can be smoked, and greens can be jarred into preserved greens, same with fruit. 

Getting other resources, like firewood, water and clothes is also required, and come winter, you really have no choice but to cross your fingers and hope you've stockpiled enough food for everyone. and won't let it spoil too quickly. 

The game takes place in what seems more like American frontier, but taking place 3-4 centuries earlier, rather than medieval Europe. Strong recommend!

Author: @thefarmerswife7575
Content:
Hey,  fun fact. Milk and eggs would likely have been less available during lent than other times of year. This is because lent always occurs in early spring, just before the time when milkcows are most likely to calve, the spring.  Yes cows can calve any time of year. But during the middle ages peasants would most likely have their cows on a springtime calving cycle since the feed would be the most abundant that time of year with meadows and pastures full of lush fresh grass.  During lent the milkcows would be producing the least amount of milk and might not even have been milked at all so that all of their energy could be devoted to ensuring the birth of a healthy calf. 
Similarly,  eggs are not as available in winter and spring because chickens are less productive in the winter because there is less daylight.  It's very possible the high cost of eggs right now is not only because of bird flu but also is a seasonal occurrence. Anyway, the restrictions on dairy and eggs during Lent might have merely reflected the fact that they didn't have these products anyway. I don't of that is definitely the reason, but I know that generally milk and egg production are down on farms during the late winter and early spring months.

Author: @chrisr251
Content: Rather than trying to cook (or even get your hands on) stock fish, look at Baccala.  That is the salted version of stock fish that also came from the same Nordic regions, during the same time period.  It became a major source of cheap protein throughout Europe during the medieval period.  And unlike stock fish, you don't need to track down some of the few producers that still make it in Norway.  You can generally find it in any well-stocked Italian market in the US.  You do, however, have to soak it both to re-hydrate it and to remove the excess salt.  If prepared well, it can have a taste and texture similar to lobster.  If prepared badly, you are better off just burning your home to the ground, as you will never get the smell out.

Author: @BogeyTheBear
Content:
The thing about sumptuary laws: You couldn't Google someone in those days to see if they were legit (actually having the job they say they have or don't have a mugshot from Florida) so material cues such as your dress and carriage were all someone might have as to inform themselves as to your social status (until subtle things like mannerisms and conversation revealed an impostor).

The violation of sumptuary laws wasn't borne out of petty jealousy, it was to prosecute a form of identity theft. Trying to establish social or business connections by wearing what is essentially a costume was considered a form of fraud, hence the criminality of dressing up all fancy when you're not of that social status.

It's cruel in light of modern meritocracy (the American Dream is the idea that anyone who is not currently a millionaire is just a millionaire-in-waiting) but they didn't have the technology we might have today to sniff out someone pretending to be something they're not (given the state of today's society, I may venture we haven't gotten the knack of it still).

One of my lecturers, who was a medieval history professor, didn't go into the details of food preservation but did make a point of reminding us that if the harvest failed that wouldn't have lead to mass starvation because people in the middle ages were skilled at preserving their food and could last through a second winter on the previous harvest. It wouldn't have been a good time and some would have died but it wouldn't have caused large scale famine, that only happened when there were multiple years of failed harvests in a row and they ran into the limits of how long grain can last/ ran through their supplies. 

It's really interesting to get to see the practical means that people used to get through the winter. It's such a good illustration of how people in the past were intelligent and skilled, just in different areas to us.

Author: @villerantavalli9395
Content:
Max, you're a bit wrong about milk -people didn't drink milk during the winter because the cows stopped giving milk in winter not just because of lent though the lack certainly made it easier to follow. Back in the middle-ages it was hard enough to gather enough hay for the animals to SURVIVE the winter -the idea of growing hay for fodder wasn't even invented before 1800s. every cent of arable land was used for growing food crops because the yields from most farmlands were abysmal by today's standards and most peasants were subsistence farmers I.e they managed to grow just about enough to feed their families, animals and pay their tax in grain and what couldn't be tilled was used for grazing or collecting wild hay for winter and a medieval domestic pig took as long as 2 years to grow into slaughter-size due to equally poor fodder as the cows got.

What fundamentally changed things was the founding & exploitation of Guano deposits of Peru -it was the first truly abundant phosphate fertilizer and tripled the yields and sometimes even five-folded them. Prior that manure and crushed limestone and wood ash were the only viable options for fertilizer.

I'm old enough to have spent my youth in a farm collecting and cutting hay by hand to know just how much hay even just a medium-sized flock of sheep would need -and that's about two smallish barns worth of hay. Cows need even more in order to keep giving milk.

Content: @12:30 The vast majority of villages in England had "common land" for common grazing, the vast majority also had fish (or eel) ponds, as well as rivers and streams. Fish was actually very common, and very very few, if any, were reliant on a "Lord's fish pond", so i'm extremely uncertain where this is supposed to apply to? At least in England this is utterly false, which is dissapointing as your channel is often accurate. In France and the HRE it could vary a lot, but you're massively underestimating the broad independence of local communities. Fish was also much more abundant in medeival times, and much easier to come by than today. Any community with a lake or on the coast, or even near a broad river was very well supplied with fish. Eels and lampreys were however much more popular than fish, due to tasting more like meat, and were in fact so popular that the east of England mainly farmed and exported Eels to the rest of England, and this had to be addressed once the protestants attempted to ban Lent. The one thing lords did usually have control over was a lot of the woodand (but again, there was usually some available as common land), and often communal mills or ovens, but by the 15th.c most communities in England had their own.

I’d love to share another traditional dish made from wheat that is still prepared in Ukraine—*kutia*. It’s a sweet Christmas dish made with boiled wheat mixed with *uzvar* (a dried fruit compote made from apples, pears, and cranberries dried over a wood fire). Author: @carolrichards5235
Content: Fasting was a little more serious during Lent back then, but I wonder if the ban on eggs & dairy may have to do a little with Lent being during late winter. Cows need to be allowed 2 months of no milking, if you want a healthy spring calf. Chickens, in my experience, usually stop laying during the short days of winter. The cows & chickens also would not be heavy producers, like the modern breeds. Yes, eggs & dairy could be preserved, but there would be a limited amount that had to last until spring, when the hens began laying again, and the cows freshened. And like today, people come down with more illnesses in winter, and the sick were allowed to eat the forbidden foods. I remember Max had a video on Medieval monks that included a bit on the monks becoming "sick" so they could avoid fasting. Probably everyday people were more likely to worry about stretching out the winter supplies, than the nobles & monks.

Author: @ahumpierrogue137
Content: Interesting note about Sumptuary laws. Basically, they existed to ensure that Merchants, who at the time were viewed as essentially getting their wealth through "cheating" people could not flaunt that wealth. In medieval times(at least in europe) the idea that Merchants can provide value was not yet really around, there was more an idea that all things had an "inherent' value. So the idea that a merchant could take something where it was less valued to somewhere it was more valued and make a profit off of that was viewed by farmers(aka 90% of the populace) and nobles alike as "cheating people" out of money. Hence the sumptuary laws to try and punish the merchants.
